title: Can Christians Date Someone Who Isn't Ready Spiritually?
paragraphs:
Can Christians Date Someone Who Isn't Ready Spiritually?
The Relationship Question That Has Broken More Hearts Than Almost Anything Else—And the Gospel Answer That Could Save Yours
You weren't planning to fall for them.
Then one day you realized your heart had quietly gone somewhere your convictions were struggling to follow.
"They don't stop me from going to church."
Maybe you've whispered those sentences to yourself.
Maybe someone whispered them to you.
Maybe you're living inside that tension right now.
And maybe what makes this even harder is that the person you're thinking about genuinely seems kind, loving, respectful, generous, and morally good.
So why does something still feel unsettled?
Because deep inside, you're asking a question that isn't really about dating.
You're asking whether love is enough to overcome spiritual direction.
That question deserves more than opinions.
It deserves the Word of God.
Because the Gospel has never been about controlling people.
It's always been about rescuing hearts.
The Bible never tells Christians to avoid people who don't yet know Christ.
Jesus Himself ate with tax collectors, sinners, prostitutes, and those rejected by society. The religious leaders criticized Him for it.
He never allowed intimacy to compromise His mission.
One of the clearest passages regarding marriage and spiritual unity comes from 2 Corinthians 6:14:
"Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?"
The word ἑτεροζυγοῦντες (heterozygountes) literally means "to be yoked together with one of a different kind."
Imagine placing one powerful ox beside a much smaller animal under the same yoke.
They don't move toward the same destination.
Both people possess equal value because both bear the image of God (Genesis 1:27).
The Bible never says Christians are better than anyone else.
It says Christians belong to Someone.
And when Christ becomes Lord, every area of life—including dating—belongs to Him.
"But what if they're open to learning?"
There is a profound difference between someone who is genuinely pursuing Christ and someone who simply appreciates that you do.
The Bible never commands believers to evangelize through romantic relationships.
Instead, Scripture repeatedly calls believers to pursue wisdom before emotional attachment clouds discernment.
"Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it."

מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ
(Mikkol mishmar netzor libbekha)
"Guard your heart with every kind of guarding."
The Hebrew word נָצַר (natsar) means to watch over carefully, preserve, protect like a treasure.
Scripture never tells us to throw our hearts into uncertainty and hope everything works out.
It tells us to guard them wisely.
Because your heart eventually shapes your future.
Some relationships don't destroy faith overnight.
Eventually Jesus moves from the center of the relationship to its background.
Not because someone forced Him out.
But because two people cannot walk toward different kingdoms forever without tension.
"Can two walk together, unless they have agreed to meet?"
Walking together in Scripture is never merely about proximity.
Imagine trying to build a lifelong marriage when one person wants to glorify Christ above everything else while the other wants Christ only when convenient.
Who decides how children are raised?
Who determines what generosity looks like?
They reach into the deepest foundation of life itself.
"But what about 1 Corinthians 7? Doesn't Paul tell believers married to unbelievers to stay married?"
Paul addresses people who came to faith after already being married.
He encourages faithfulness within existing marriages if the unbelieving spouse is willing to remain.
He is not encouraging Christians to intentionally enter spiritually divided marriages.
There is a difference between remaining faithful in a difficult situation and deliberately choosing one.
God also calls believers to wisdom before entering covenant.
Then there is one of the most beautiful biblical love stories.

Before Isaac married, Abraham instructed his servant not to take a wife from the surrounding Canaanite peoples who worshiped other gods (Genesis 24). The concern was not ethnicity but covenant faithfulness. The unfolding story emphasizes God's providence in bringing together two people within His redemptive purposes.
Throughout Scripture, God's concern is consistently about wholehearted devotion to Him.
That concern reaches its climax in the words of Jesus:
"Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness..."

ζητεῖτε δὲ πρῶτον τὴν βασιλείαν
(zēteite de prōton tēn basileian)
The word πρῶτον (prōton) means first—not merely first in sequence, but first in priority, rank, and supremacy.
Everything else belongs beneath His reign.
Perhaps this article feels painfully personal.
Maybe you're dating someone who isn't ready spiritually.
Maybe you're praying they will change.
Maybe they even promise they will.
The Gospel itself is the greatest testimony that Jesus rescues sinners.
But wisdom refuses to build lifelong decisions on hoped-for future transformation that has not yet become present reality.
That is not a lack of faith.
And if you're the one who isn't spiritually ready, hear this clearly:
This article is not pushing you away from Jesus.
It is inviting you to Him.
Christ did not come for spiritually impressive people.
For every person who knows life isn't working without Him.
"But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
Grace always arrives before we deserve it.
Every one of us has been spiritually unready apart from Christ.
He bore our sin upon the cross.
He rose again, conquering death, so that everyone who repents and believes in Him might receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Ephesians 2:8–9).
That is why our theme is more than a slogan.
From Scandal to Grace. Because Jesus Rewrites Everything.
Perhaps today, the greatest relationship decision you need to make is not whether to pursue another person.
It is whether to surrender fully to Jesus Christ.
Every healthy Christian relationship begins there.

In that sense, supporting this work is one practical way to participate in spreading the Gospel and glorifying God through faithful stewardship, while always remembering that God's glory is never something we purchase but something we seek to honor with generous hearts.
One surrendered heart today can become the testimony that rescues another tomorrow.
